output.headline: Government reaffirms 2035 zero-emissions car target amid mandate review
output.bodyHtml:
Ministers are set to keep the government's 2035 deadline for all new cars to be zero emission, even as they prepare to ease the nearer-term electric vehicle (EV) sales target this week, in a move that will relieve carmakers but alarm many Labour MPs who are worried about the government's commitment to the green agenda.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalise the plan after a crunch meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday to settle a long-running dispute between the transport, energy and business departments.

Haigh is expected to agree to cut a target for EV sales by about a quarter, government sources say, helping British industry but setting up a potential fight with MPs and campaigners over the government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy.

The decision will be made just as Andy Burnham prepares to travel to his first Cop summit as prime minister, where he and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will champion electrification on a global scale.

With some MPs already upset by the decisions to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and to cut funding for green schemes to pay for higher defence spending, many see the upcoming decisions on the Rosebank oilfield and the EV mandate as critically important.

Lizzi Collinge, the Labour MP for Morecambe and Lunesdale, said: “The upcoming decision on the ZEV [zero emission vehicle] mandate will have a huge climate impact, possibly the biggest one that’s on the PM’s desk.

“But it will also set the direction for tackling the cost of living and helping get our energy prices down over the coming decade.”

Catherine Fookes, the MP for Monmouthshire, said: “The government has some incredibly difficult decisions to make in the coming months and the prime minister will need to weigh up the consequences of each. We need the ZEV mandate to stay, and Rosebank to be rejected.”

A government spokesperson said: “The government is united in its commitment to the ZEV mandate and no decisions have been taken.

“We are committed to the phaseout of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets.

“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this, and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

Under rules brought in by the last Conservative government, carmakers have to make sure they only sell EVs by 2035, gradually increasing the proportion over time to 80% by 2030.

The policy is expected to create greater emissions savings than any other, leading to nearly 14% of all the reductions to which the UK has pledged between 2028 and 2032.

Carmakers say the interim targets in particular are unattainable, arguing that higher inflation and a squeeze on living standards have pushed them out of reach.

The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) says the industry will miss this year’s 33% target by a wide margin, with battery EVs accounting for 26.6% of new car sales in the first 10 months of the year.

Those targets, however, do not take into account exemptions that allow carmakers to avoid fines even if they undershoot their targets, such as by selling more hybrid cars, or making up for lower sales of electric cars now by selling more in the future.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The gap between demand and mandated targets continues to widen.

“Meaningful change to the trajectory, alongside expanded flexibilities throughout the regulation, is essential to bridge that gap, safeguard jobs and investment while keeping the UK’s zero emission transition on track.”

Ministers have adjusted the targets on multiple occasions since the policy was first proposed, and the government launched another review into the policy in August, proposing five main options.

They were: to keep the mandate unchanged; keep it at 80% but extend the flexibilities by four years to 2034; reduce the interim target to 70%; reduce it to 60%; or reduce it to 50%.

That consultation kickstarted an internal debate in Whitehall. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has argued for the 2030 target to be reduced as far as possible, to 50%.

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, is believed to want it to be approximately 60%, while Miatta Fahnbulleh and her predecessor as energy secretary, Ed Miliband, are understood to want it to remain at 80%.

The prime minister would normally have sought to resolve the dispute himself, but Burnham has recused himself from the decision because his wife, Marie-France van Heel, advises the board of the Manchester-based electric vehicle charging network Be.EV.

Related: U-turn on EV policy could stall UK’s take-up of EVs | Fiona Harvey and Jasper Jolly

Government insiders say Haigh will probably settle on a 2030 target of about 60% rather than the deeper cuts some had pushed for, while also extending the flexibilities in the targets until 2034. She is understood to have told colleagues, however, that she does not want them to come back in the future demanding another target reduction.

The decision will nonetheless upset some Labour MPs, and will also dismay people in the wider environmental movement and in the EV charging industry, which is relying on high vehicle sales to recoup investment.

Shane Brennan, the chief executive of the trade association ChargeUK, said: “Weakening the mandate puts £1.7bn of charging infrastructure at risk and all the associated jobs and supply chain spending that goes with it.

“Charging investors’ confidence will be rocked by a third change in three years. Government should be in no way complacent about the long-term implications of being seen to cave to the short-term interest of global car importers.”

Paul McNamee, the director of the Labour Climate and Environment Forum, said: “Significant weakening of the ZEV mandate from the current 80% targets will be seen as a rowing back on climate leadership.

“If the government does this, it must provide assurance that the mandate will not be weakened again in the coming years, the 2035 target for EVs remains in place, and it delivers a robust industrial strategy to build a strong EV manufacturing base in the UK that will protect jobs in the long term.”

Additional reporting by Jasper Jolly
output.standfirst:
Exclusive: Ministers plan to keep the 2035 zero-emissions deadline in place even as Louise Haigh eases the 2030 electric vehicle sales target, a trade-off Labour MPs are pushing back against

  • Analysis: Climate always comes second – are green issues slipping down Burnham's agenda?
output.progress: Haigh is resisting the business department's push to cut the 2030 target as low as 50%, and has told colleagues she wants no further reductions.

output.headline: Eisenkot reaches out across Israel's divide in bid to form government
output.bodyHtml:
Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic state of emergency.

Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority.

“We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the state of Israel,” said Eisenkot, who had traded his usual all black for a suit and tie at a ceremony at the presidential office. “We must form a national emergency government. This will require creative and unconventional political steps.”

Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.

Eisenkot and Herzog acknowledged Israel’s growing isolation under Netanyahu, who is wanted by the international criminal court.

In the US, Israel’s closest ally, Democrats on Tuesday swept the midterm elections, with calls to rein in Israel after the devastation in Gaza and the unpopular Iran war, which Netanyahu launched with Donald Trump.

Eisenkot said: “We are in the midst of a devastating diplomatic crisis. Even our closest friends and strategic allies are saying their relationship with Israel must be reassessed.”

He appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud party as well as the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, to join him – but only with himself as prime minister.

“My door is open and my hand is extended, wholeheartedly and willingly, to anyone who understands the gravity of this moment,” he said.

Related: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu

Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.

Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in the October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.

During party consultations with Herzog, Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.

Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of his partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, has already said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.

Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims.

Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Committee – and Herzog – say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing was found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.

Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night but it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement. These types of coalition governments are notoriously fragile and often collapse.

Related: Donald Trump’s power is on the wane. What next for Russia, Israel – and the rest of us? | Simon Tisdall

Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.

He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.

He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and has vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.

Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.

After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.

If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.
output.standfirst: The former military chief is appealing to rivals across the political spectrum to build a national unity government, after saying Netanyahu has brought Israel to a state of emergency nearing a 'point of no return'
output.progress: Eisenkot has received endorsements from both Arab-majority party lists and is reaching out to Netanyahu's allies to try to build a coalition.

context.text: Israel's election commission has confirmed the vote's results and rejected claims of mass fraud promoted by Netanyahu.

output.headline: Nvidia opens independent investigation into Huang's conduct and security ties
output.bodyHtml:
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.

The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”

Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”

Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.

Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.

The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.

“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.

Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.

“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.

The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.

Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.

Related: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports

However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.

US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.

The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.

The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.

A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting
output.standfirst: Nvidia's board says it is examining Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a Chinese businesswoman accused of passing information to Beijing, after the CEO admitted to an affair and said there was 'no excuse' for his actions
output.progress: Nvidia's board says it has found no sign yet that national security or trade secrets were compromised, and will continue its review.

output.headline: GPs to give 300,000 vulnerable patients extra support this winter
output.bodyHtml:
Hundreds of thousands of vulnerable patients in England are to receive extra support from their GP as part of a £40m drive aimed at keeping them out of hospital this winter.

As the NHS gears up for the pressures of the coming months, family doctors will offer 300,000 people with frailty and long-term conditions health checks, medication reviews and respiratory tests designed to prevent avoidable hospital admissions.

Funded by cash reallocated from existing GP budgets for 2026-27, the scheme will allow surgeries to identify and provide extra care to the patients they believe are most at risk of becoming seriously unwell in the winter. Groups of GP practices can use £126 for every eligible patient supported.

The prime minister said the scheme would be targeted at patients with heart disease, frailty and lung conditions such as emphysema and other types of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Andy Burnham said he was “not going to pretend this winter will be easy” but the programme would help keep people well at home and avoid unnecessary trips to hospital.

“If we want to take the pressure off our hospitals this winter, we’ve got to keep people well at home. So we’re backing GPs to reach the most vulnerable people early, before a small problem turns into a trip to A&E,” he said.

“People deserve the right care in the right place. And our NHS staff, who work so hard, deserve the right tools to provide it. I’m not going to pretend this winter will be easy. But with new technology, upgrades for hospitals and more care available closer to home, we’ll make sure the NHS is there for everyone when they need it.”

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said the scheme had been designed to offer greater support to the frailest patients.

“After such a heavy summer for our NHS as a result of the heat, everyone is working together to prepare for more challenging winter pressures,” she said. “That includes the rollout of flu vaccinations, investing in extra urgent care capacity and strengthening partnerships with social care.

“With thousands more GPs in post and millions more GP appointments this year, the £40m programme to support vulnerable patients in the community is part of our plan to help patients, improve primary care and also to support our NHS through the heavier winter months.”

Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, the president of the Royal College of GPs, said she welcomed the focus on prevention and supporting patients at greatest risk of avoidable hospital admission this winter.

“GPs’ clinical expertise, knowledge of their patients and continuity of care are central to identifying those most in need and providing personalised, coordinated support,” she said.

But she also said short-term initiatives alone could not deliver “sustained improvements in care” that patients with complex health needs required. Instead, she said, a longer-term approach to prevention was necessary, which must be backed by “sustainable investment in general practice”.
output.standfirst: A £40m scheme in England will let GP surgeries carry out health checks, medication reviews and respiratory tests for the most vulnerable, aiming to prevent unnecessary hospital admissions as winter pressures mount on the NHS
output.progress: The scheme is funded by cash reallocated from existing GP budgets, letting surgeries offer extra care worth £126 per eligible patient.

output.headline: NHS 10-year plan aims to reduce premature heart and stroke deaths by a quarter
output.bodyHtml:
Fewer than one in 15 stroke survivors are getting the amount of therapy the NHS should provide to maximise their chances of recovery, a report has revealed.

The figure was a “damning” indictment of the widespread lack of rehabilitation for patients, which was hindering their chances of regaining physical and mental function, the Stroke Association said.

Only 6.4% of those in England, Wales and Northern Ireland who have a stroke receive the three hours a day of rehabilitation therapy at least five days a week to which they are entitled.

The finding is disclosed in the latest annual report of the Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme (SSNAP), which is based on stroke care data from hospitals in the three countries.

Almost 100,000 people a year in the UK have a stroke. It is the single largest cause of complex disability and can leave survivors struggling to walk, talk or swallow. The ageing population, and an increased number of people with high blood pressure or diabetes, could cause the annual figure to rise to 115,483 by 2030.

All stroke patients should get three hours of physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, and occupational therapy to help them recover from the brain injury they have suffered, whether they are still in hospital or have returned home to continue their rehabilitation.

That is set out in National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines intended to guide NHS practice in England and Wales. They are also followed in Northern Ireland.

However, during January to March this year – the latest figures available – only 6.4% of patients received that amount, down from the 7.5% who did so in October to December 2024.

The average amount of therapy stroke survivors in the three countries received in the first quarter of this year was 40 minutes, six minutes less than in late 2024. Some patients received only 15.2 minutes, while the maximum received was still only 57.3 minutes, the SSNAP audit showed.

In addition, only 68% of patients received continuing help with their rehabilitation once they had been discharged from hospital, the report found.

“These damning figures expose the deeply troubling reality that too many vulnerable stroke survivors are being left without the care and support they need, both in the critical days after their stroke and in the months and years that follow,” said Juliet Bouverie, the Stroke Association’s chief executive.

“The brain injury caused by stroke can change every aspect of a person’s life in an instant and last for a lifetime. Stroke is both a medical emergency and a long-term condition which touches on almost every aspect of NHS and social care.

“Yet too often, our health and care system focuses on treating the emergency rather than considering the importance of what comes after that – and these shocking statistics reveal the true extent of that.”

Bouverie said services for stroke survivors “are already overstretched to breaking point” as the charity published a new report showing that stroke costs the UK an estimated £25.7bn a year.

More than half that sum (£13.7bn) goes on the social care costs of helping survivors. The wider societal costs, such as people no longer being able to work and relatives having to give up work to care for survivors, amount to another £6.7bn. Welfare benefits to patients and income tax not collected because they had had to stop work came to £2.4bn alone, the charity estimated.

The Department of Health and Social Care did not comment on the overwhelming majority of stroke patients not receiving enough rehabilitation. Instead it stressed the NHS’s efforts to improve care.

“Hundreds of people every day suffer a stroke, and the NHS is working hard to get them the rapid support and long-term rehabilitation they will often require,” a spokesperson said.

“In our 10-year health plan last year, we pledged to reduce premature mortality from heart disease and stroke by a quarter within a decade, and our cardiovascular disease modern service framework, published in July, aims to accelerate that progress.

“The NHS is also working to increase the delivery of thrombolysis and thrombectomy rates as a key intervention to support improved outcomes in patients who have had a stroke,” they added.
output.standfirst: The government points to its 10-year plan to reduce premature deaths from heart disease and stroke by a quarter, after a report found just 6.4% of survivors get the rehabilitation therapy they are entitled to
output.progress: The NHS says it is working to increase thrombolysis and thrombectomy rates and published a new cardiovascular care framework in July.

context.text: The NHS is rolling out free high-street cholesterol tests in England, the first of their kind globally, to spot stroke and heart disease risks earlier.

output.headline: Trump offers Democrats a deal to let some long-term migrants stay
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump has offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats, a concession following the Republicans’ heavy defeat in the midterm elections, in which he also admitted that his deportation policy was “too tough”.

In an interview on the CBS network’s 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, the president acknowledged that the aggressive crackdown had hurt him politically and said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.

Trump was asked by 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether his deportation policy had gone too far. “I think it was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”

Related: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making UFC’s Dana White next press secretary

The president’s comments offered an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. They came, however, just two days after he elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

Since Trump returned to office, sweeping Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids at workplaces, homes and public spaces have ensnared people with no criminal records, separated families and spread fear in immigrant communities. Federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The president said his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Trump added that there were competing views within the country about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported or allowed to remain if they were working and paying taxes. He said some people believed that “they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company” and “in some cases, paying taxes”.

Trump said he believed an agreement with Democrats was achievable, allowing some long-term undocumented residents to stay while continuing to remove people convicted of serious crimes. He proposed targeting killers, rapists and drug dealers while making an accommodation for people who had been in the country for 10 or 15 years.

“Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said. He described the proposal as something that could be negotiated, saying: “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

Trump said Democrats appeared receptive to a compromise, adding that some had already contacted him. Asked whether he could refrain from name-calling for six months to secure an agreement, he replied: “Very easily.”

Related: Trump’s shattered ‘mirror world’: American voters roundly reject president’s alternate reality

Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat, agreeing with an assessment by his vice-president, JD Vance, that the conflict had been a major factor. He also cited what he described as growing dislike of Israel.

He maintained, however, that the military campaign had been justified and said he would make the same decision again. “My answer is an emphatic yes because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

Trump insisted the war had been won and predicted that Tehran would eventually negotiate a deal. He acknowledged that the military campaign might not have been popular in the short term, saying: “I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.”

He said he was not looking to escalate the conflict after the midterms.

On the economy, the president conceded that his administration had failed to communicate its achievements effectively, despite repeatedly claiming that employment, investment and stock market figures were at record levels. “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me,” he said.

Trump signalled an openness to safeguards for artificial intelligence, having previously favoured allowing technology companies to police themselves rather than imposing sweeping government restrictions. “I don’t mind guardrails,” he told 60 Minutes. “But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position.”

The interview also raised questions about the substantial increase in Trump’s personal wealth since his return to the White House.

Douthat cited a Forbes estimate that Trump’s net worth had increased by $3bn from the autumn of 2024 to the autumn of 2025. Trump initially suggested that the increase reflected the general performance of the stock market and said his finances were managed by his son.

Asked about his family’s cryptocurrency business, World Liberty Financial, in which he is a co-owner and which has attracted investment from people connected to the United Arab Emirates, Trump defended the arrangement by saying: “I know nothing about it.”

But Dan Alexander, a Forbes senior editor who calculates the net worth of wealthy individuals for the magazine, challenged Trump’s explanation in a lengthy thread on X, arguing that the president’s increased fortune could not be explained simply by stock market gains.

Alexander identified several sources including cryptocurrency ventures that generated more than $1bn in proceeds and the appreciation of tokens retained by Trump, overseas licensing agreements that expanded the value of his branding business, and the removal of an almost $500m financial penalty in his New York civil fraud case.

Trump also offered a glimpse of the Republican succession battle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, saying he might endorse a candidate but had not decided whether to intervene. Asked whether he expected to endorse a successor, Trump replied: “Probably. Not necessarily.”

He described the Republican party as having a strong field of potential candidates and praised secretary of state Marco Rubio while declining to rule out other contenders.

The president said his endorsement would carry considerable weight but suggested he might be better off staying out of the contest. He also expressed confidence that the “Make America great again” movement could survive without him as its leader, describing its defining principles as strong borders and a strong military.

At the end of the interview, Trump was asked whether he could forgive political opponents including former FBI director James Comey and former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, even before the judgment of God. Trump said: “The answer is no. I want to be honest, no.”

Douthat followed up: “Mr President. You have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime and you are telling me that before the judgment throne of God you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies? After all that’s been given to you? Come on. Help me out here.”

But Trump remained adamant, insisting: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”

Douthat then noted that many presidents are remembered with a single line such as “He freed the slaves” or “He won the cold war” and asked what line will Trump’s presidency be remembered with.

The president said simply: “That I made America great again.”
output.standfirst: After the midterms, the president offered to negotiate letting some long-term undocumented immigrants with jobs remain in the US, acknowledging his deportation policy — during which agents fatally shot two US citizens — was 'too tough'
output.progress: Trump says Democrats have already reached out, and that an agreement protecting long-settled immigrants while still removing serious criminals is 'actually doable'.

output.headline: Maya Jama leaves Love Island to pursue new opportunities after nine seasons
output.bodyHtml:
Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of Love Island after three years.

The 32-year-old presenter of the reality TV show made the announcement on Instagram.

Posting a highlights reel of herself on the programme, Jama said it was “time to throw myself into something new”.

“While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I’ll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever,” the TV and radio presenter said.

The move comes after Jama’s stint on the BBC’s Celebrity Traitors, as a traitor who breezed through the series undetected until the finale. Her popularity led to speculation in the Times that she could “get £1m per deal” thanks to her success.

Jama took over from Laura Whitmore as the host when the show returned for its ninth series early in 2023.

Related: ‘Adversity can ruin your life. Or give you resilience’: Maya Jama on grit, growing up, and bringing good vibes to primetime tv

She was initially touted as a potential host after it was confirmed Caroline Flack would be stepping down as host in 2019, but the role was given to Whitmore.

Thanking fans and the production team on Love Island, she said she had an “unforgettable time” on the programme.

“I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the nine incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I’ve loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show.”

But she added: “I’ve always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then.”

An ITV spokesperson said: “Maya has been a fantastic and much-loved host on Love Island – we thank her for everything she has brought to the show over the last three years and wish her every continued success.”

Jama moved to London when she was aged 16 to pursue a career in the entertainment industry. She began her broadcasting work co-hosting Trending Live on 4Music and Cannonball on ITV, before moving to present her BBC Radio 1 show on Fridays and Saturdays.

At 23, she became the youngest person to co-host the Mobo awards on Channel 5 in 2017, alongside the JLS star turned presenter Marvin Humes.
output.standfirst: The 32-year-old presenter says it's 'time to throw myself into something new', thanking fans for an 'unforgettable time' hosting nine series of the dating show

output.headline: Godzilla Minus Zero sets box office records in blockbuster US debut
output.bodyHtml:
Japan’s most recognisable film star shows no sign of losing its ability to captivate global audiences, after Godzilla Minus Zero – a foreign language film - swept to the top of the US box office on its opening weekend.

The film – the 39th in a franchise stretching back to 1954 – generated $63m worldwide, including $31.6m in the US and Canada, where it set a record for opening weekend receipts for the biggest live-action foreign-language film. It is shown in Japanese with English subtitles.

Filmgoers were just as enthralled in Japan, where the sequel to the 2003 Oscar-winning film Godzilla Minus One set a domestic record for a live-action film, according to the Kyodo news agency.

In Godzilla Minus Zero, set in Japan in 1949 – two years after it lay “dead” at the bottom of the ocean – the creature resurfaced to respond to a new threat to the country’s attempts to rebuild after the second world war: a dragon-like beast called Ghidorah.

Related: Godzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise’s winning streak

The film, directed by Takashi Yamazaki, shows a radioactively regenerated Godzilla confront its three-headed nemesis – which destroys buildings with lightning bolts fired from its mouth – with the help of human intervention.

“This historic opening shows how deeply audiences around the world connect with Godzilla and with Takashi Yamazaki’s vision,” Koji Ueda, president of Toho Global, which produced the film, said in a statement. “Our first near-simultaneous global release was built on that belief.”

In Japan, Godzilla earned ($5.75m) on its opening day on 3 November, setting a box office revenue record for the first day of a live-action release in the country and, according to Toho, more than double the opening day earnings generated by Godzilla Minus One.

Minus Zero qualifies as a live-action film as it was principally shot on-location, including at a sports park in Ibaraki, northeast of Tokyo, that was used for large crowd scenes and at a temple in Maizuru, Kyoto prefecture.

Industry experts said the success of its global release on Imax and regular screens worldwide had easily exceeded expectations.

“This weekend’s opening takes the Japanese production to a new level – it’s nearly three times the previous opening [of Godzilla Minus One] in December 2023,” industry analyst David A Gross wrote.

The latest Godzilla film faces competition from the Indian epic Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, which earned $55.7m on its opening weekend. The Hindi-language blockbuster – the most expensive Indian film ever made – made $8.7m in the US and $32m in India.

Godzilla Minus Zero and Ramayana were produced in the Imax format, with the former receiving an early Imax-only release last week. The large-format screens appear to have driven audience interest, generating 34% of Godzilla’s box office take on its opening weekend.
output.standfirst: The Japanese film topped the North American box office with $31.6m in its opening weekend, generating $63m worldwide and breaking records in Japan too
